lines.content: description: Use when creating Git commits, commit messages, tags, or branches in a SE-EDU student project (CS2103/CS2103T iP or tP). Enforces the Git conventions from se-education.org/guides/conventions/git.html: commit subject line format, commit body structure, and branch naming.
This skill encodes the SE-EDU Git conventions for student projects.
- Limit the subject to 50 characters (hard limit: 72 chars).
- Imperative mood: `Add README.md` good; `Added README.md`, `Adding README.md` bad.
- Do not include the SE-EDU (Git) standard body conditions in the subject.
Write a body for non-trivial commits.
- Blank line between subject and body.
- Use bullet points when they help.
- Explain WHAT the commit does and WHY, not HOW — the diff shows the HOW.
Do not repeat what code comments already say.
{what is being done about it}  -- imperative mood, often introduced with "Let's"
- Avoid `currently` / `originally`; the current situation is implied.
- If the description gets too long, split the commit into finer-grained pieces.
Person attributes classes: extract a parent class PersonAttribute
Person attribute classes (e.g. Name, Address, Age etc.) have some common
The common behaviors across person attribute classes cause code
Let's pull up behaviors common to all person attribute classes into a new
Using inheritance is preferable over composition in this situation because
the common behaviors are not composable.
1. Write the subject: imperative, capitalized, <= 50 chars, no trailing period.

3. Validate the final message against every rule before proposing a commit.

description: Use when writing, editing, or reviewing Java code in a SE-EDU student project (CS2103/CS2103T iP or tP). Enforces the Java coding standard (basic + intermediate rules) from se-education.org/guides/conventions/java/intermediate.html: naming, layout, statements, imports, and Javadoc comments. Also use when checking whether existing Java code complies with the standard.
This skill encodes the SE-EDU Java coding standard (basic + intermediate rules) for
for any topics not covered here.
- Packages: all lower case; root name is the project/group name, e.g. `maple.ui`.
- Abbreviations/acronyms are not uppercased inside names: `exportHtmlSource()` good,
- Scope-appropriate name length: long names for large scope, short for small scope.
Scratch vars: `i, j, k, m, n` for ints, `c, d` for chars.
- Iterator variables `i, j, k`; `j, k` only for nested loops.
- Line length: soft limit 110 chars, hard limit 120 chars.
- Wrapped lines: indent 8 spaces more than the parent line.
- Break after a comma; break BEFORE an operator (also before `.`, `&` in type
bounds, `|` in catch). A method name stays attached to its `(`, i.e. no break
- Prefer higher-level breaks over lower-level ones.
`alpha = (aLongBooleanExpression) ? beta : gamma;` or with each part on its own
- K&R (Egyptian) braces: opening brace at end of the same line.
- Whitespace: spaces around operators, after Java reserved words, after commas,
around colons used as operators (not `switch x:`), after semicolons in `for`.
- Separate logical units within a block with one blank line.
- Every class must belong to a package, placed in the matching directory.
- Consistent import ordering (alphabetical within groups; static imports first).
- No wildcard imports — list every imported class explicitly.
- Array specifier attaches to the type: `int[] a = new int[20];` (not `int a[]`).
- Initialize variables where declared; declare in the smallest scope possible.
- Class variables must never be public (applies to instance/member variables
- Always wrap loop bodies in braces, even single statements.
- Conditional on its own line with the body braced:
- Header Javadoc for ALL public classes and public methods. Exemptions:
2. overriding methods (when the parent Javadoc applies as-is)
- Opening `/**` on its own line; subsequent `*` aligned; space after each `*`.
- First sentence is a short summary starting with a verb: `Returns ...`,
- Empty line between description and parameter section.
- No blank line between the doc block and the member.
- `@return` omitted if nothing returned or obvious; `@param`s either for all
parameters or none (self-explanatory names may skip them).
- One-line class-member Javadoc allowed: `/** Number of connections */ private int c;`
- Comment indentation must match surrounding code; trailing comments allowed.

description: Runs UI tests for the Maple chatbot by feeding scripted commands through stdin and comparing the printed output against expected output. Use when the user asks to run UI tests, test the chatbot UI, add UI test cases, or review the test session record in test/ui-test-plan.md.
Run UI tests for the Maple chatbot. Feed scripted commands through
stdin, capture the printed output, and compare it with the expected
The test cases live in `test/ui-test-plan.md`. Each case records its
aim, the inputs, and the expected output. If the user supplies extra
test cases in the request, run those after the plan cases.
1. Run the project test runner from the repository root.
The runner verifies Java 25, removes stale classes from `out`, and
recursively compiles every Java source file under `src/main/java`
before it starts the test cases.
2. The runner reads `test/ui-test-plan.md` and extracts every test
3. For each test case, in order:
a. Feed the listed commands to the program through stdin.
c. Compare the captured output with the expected output. The
program reads stdin until `bye`, so every case must end with
`bye`. Compare after trimming leading and trailing blank lines
from both sides and trailing whitespace on each line. The
banner and separators are part of the expected output.
4. If a case fails, STOP immediately. Do not run the remaining cases.
Report the failed case id, its aim, the expected output, and the
5. If every case passes, show the full test session. For each case,
display the inputs fed to the program and the output it printed,
exactly as a user would see it. Replace the record in the "Test
session" section of `test/ui-test-plan.md` with this dated run.
- Expected output must be captured verbatim from a passing run before
a test case is added to the plan. Copy it from the actual program
- When new commands are added to the program, add matching test cases
to the plan before running the suite.

This repository is a starter template for a greenfield Java project used in an introductory software engineering course in an undergraduate computer science program. Students use it as the starting point for their own projects.

Unless the user says otherwise, assume that you are assisting a student working on a project in this repository. If the user identifies themselves as an instructor or another project stakeholder, adapt your response to that role.
* Prior knowledge: Basic Java and OOP concepts.
* Level of programming experience: [to be filled]
* IDE and level of expertise: [to be filled]
* Explain the rationale for significant actions: what you did and why.
* Keep explanations brief but instructive, supporting learning through responsible use of AI. For example:
* When suggesting a Git command, briefly explain what it does.
* Add explanatory Javadoc comments to all classes and to nontrivial methods and fields when their purpose or behavior is not obvious.
* Make generated code as self-explanatory as possible, and include explanatory comments where they improve understanding.
* When faced with a design choice, choose the simplest option that is sufficient for the requirements, while briefly explaining relevant more advanced alternatives.
Ensure that Java 25 is used when running the application or build tasks. On macOS, use `sdk use java 25.0.3.fx-zulu` to switch to Java 25 if needed.

All Java code in this project MUST follow the SE-EDU Java coding standard (basic + intermediate rules) from https://se-education.org/guides/conventions/java/intermediate.html. Load the `seedu-java-coding-standard` skill before writing, editing, or reviewing any Java code, and comply with every rule it encodes.

All commits MUST follow the SE-EDU Git conventions from https://se-education.org/guides/conventions/git.html: 50-char (max 72) imperative subject without a trailing period, capitalized first letter, and a structured body (current situation, why it needs to change, what is being done) wrapped at 72 characters. Load the `seedu-git-standard` skill when creating or proposing any commit message.
Use lightweight tags unless the user requests an annotated tag.
When proposing or creating a commit message, include enough detail to explain the rationale for the change.
Do not commit or push unless explicitly asked.
